attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his 2026 predictions post.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will escalate' forecast for 2026. The normalised claim keeps both targets, and the separate midterm and Trump sentences are rightly excluded.

contract.note: The plain reading (more opposition in 2026 than in 2025) is ordinary and fair. Inferring a US focus from the surrounding context is reasonable.

evidence.note: The May 2026 Gallup survey shows Americans cooling toward AI. It covers AI in general, not generative AI or deregulation, and it is not a full-year measure.
The March 2026 Quinnipiac poll shows some measures largely unchanged since 2025. It does not isolate opposition to deregulation.

reviews.rationale: The horizon runs to 2026-12-31, after the evaluation date. The polls give only partial, general-AI direction, which does not meet the early-resolution rule. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own retrospective on 2025 in the same post.

semantics.note: A bundled observation: two factual parts (no AGI; hallucinations not solved) plus a subjective judgment ('underwhelming').

contract.note: Reading 'not solved' as 'persisted' rather than 'did not improve' is fair. The contract rightly declines to invent a benchmark for 'underwhelming', and AGI has no definition.

evidence.note: OpenAI says GPT-5 still hallucinates (September 2025). It is a company disclosure but an admission against its own interest, and it directly bears on the hallucination part.
The December 2025 ARC Prize report says new ideas are still needed for AGI. This fits the no-AGI part but is not a comprehensive determination.
OpenAI reports that GPT-5 has fewer hallucinations. Improvement does not mean the problem is solved and does not settle whether GPT-5 met expectations.

reviews.rationale: The hallucination part holds: OpenAI acknowledged that GPT-5 still hallucinated. The no-AGI part is consistent with the ARC Prize assessment but not fully established. 'Underwhelming' is a value judgment with no stated standard, so it is not adjudicable.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will be' forecast for 2026. 'Human domestic robots' is fairly read as humanoid home robots.

contract.note: The plain reading (few units delivered to homes, many demos) is ordinary. Using thousands of home deliveries as the early-contradiction threshold is a reasonable reading of 'very little product'.

evidence.note: An April 2026 report says 1X NEO shipments were still expected, with partial teleoperation (remote human control). It shows no large-scale home delivery but cannot settle the full year.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2026-12-31, after the evaluation date. No evidence documents thousands of home deliveries, so the early-contradiction rule is not met. Support can only be judged after year-end.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement in his retrospective on 2025.

semantics.note: An observation about December 2025. 'The economics look dubious' is an evaluative appearance claim with no measure.

contract.note: Reading 'reliable' as dependable without literal perfection is fair. Treating the economic clause as untestable without a defined measure is also fair.

evidence.note: The December 2025 GPT-5.2 release admits remaining errors and advises users to double-check critical answers. It covers one model, is a company disclosure, and is not representative across LLMs.

reviews.rationale: The reliability clause has only partial support from one developer's disclosure. The contract requires representative evaluations across common uses, which are absent. The economic clause names no financial measure and cannot be scored. Together the evidence does not settle the claim.
